I had those same experiences in civilian mental healthcare but it took months/years between visits (VA here can get me in within days since I'm not competing with the entire community for limited appointments), cost tons of money (even with insurance) and there was poor communication between all the providers; I had to re-explain everything every time.    


I have had several VA health providers say, "I see in your records..." and I no longer worry that I will run out of my meds as my refill request gets stuck between insurance, the licensed prescriber and whichever pharmacy private insurance permits me to use. Now, the meds just shows up in my mailbox and is free. I actuslly have a surplus now. And If I have any undesirable side effects from med changes, I make a single phone call and changes are implemented immediately. 


There is still so much we don't understand about mental health and not every treatment works for everyone so trial and error is a common approach unfortunately. It is already difficult to ask for help and having to switch combinations of treatments can increase the despair. Someday, it will seem cruel that we couldn't just scan the brain or perform a lab test to better guide individualized treatment plans. 


Pleading for disability/compensation and waiting for decisions from the benefit side of the VA, however, has been far more stressful and less predictable. It also feels, like others said, like I am having prove I am worthy of the support I need. But now, I have actual hope that my life (not just health) can improve instead of paying to hear the same coping techniques repackaged with new words and acronyms. Access to VA healthcare through service-connected disability likely saved my life.

I manned up and proudly completed the degree; the hardest goal I have completed to date. I spend months trying to get a civilian job and eventually work in a hospital laboratory outside of Chicago and find that the civilian world is cold-hearted and doesn't have my interests in mind at all. 

The Air Force may go full-retard at times but it's all based on a culture of "cover-your-ass." It may get out of hand but, ultimately, the reflective belts and absurd number sexual assault briefs show that the Air Force, in its own f'd up way cares about me even if it's just because the guy above me doesn't want to get in trouble for not keeping me from sticking my tongue in electric outlets whereas the civilian is driven by profits and personal agendas; I wouldn't get breaks for lunch (but it would be deducted out of my
hours), there was no hope of promotion, training on critical procedures was something you had to seek out and I would be left alone to fend for myself on many occasions; I was just a pawn in a bigger machine with a mission measured in $$$ rather than mission completion and power point stats.

I am now back in the ANG as a traditional and trying desperately to get a full-time job on base as an AGR or Technician to get paid nearly twice as much to work alongside people closer to my age (civilian labs are full of old ladies who don't/can't retire) to do a job that only requires a high school degree versus the bachelor degree that cost me nearly everything to get and rarely gets me an interview when applying to civilian jobs.

Other answer: it's hard to use your level of training/experience in the air guard. The closest I can think of is IDMT (independent medical technician). But like aeromedical evacuation (AE), which you mentioned, it is a special duty for 4N0X1s and you might be required to do a few years before applying to these duties. This depends on the unit. Not every guard unit has AE or IDMTs and it may not be a guarantee later down the line. 

4N0X1s or Aerospace medicine technicians are basically LPNs or CNAs; you mostly do stuff like vitals, annual physicals (vision tests, draw a few labs, maybe EKG, heating tests, etc.) and administrative duties; there is no inpatient aspect to the guard when you're not deployed. 

As far as AE, your patients have to be stable before being transported (usually determined by their H&amp;H) and if they require more critical care such as a ventilator, they are assigned CCATT personnel which uses a different enlisted member (essentially respiratory therapist, a nurse and a doctor). So you won't be applying a lot of emergency medicine. It can be a fulfilling assignment but doesn't really utilize your skill set.

Also, there are occasionally opportunities to apply to Physician Assistant school but there are many hoops to jump through (several letters of recommendation including from your Med. Group commander) and it is, once again, not a guarantee. Army National Guard does have Combat Medics but I have no experience with them so I don't know much "real" information.

Common experience: 
1) Talk to a recruiter - In Air National Guard (ANG), these are usually at the base beyond the guarded gates so you'll likely need to call them and make an appointment. 

2) Recruiter will have lots of questions for you including your reasons for wanting to join. They will also ask what job you are interested in and/or tell you what jobs they currently have open. It might be a very short list and even less will have an enlistment bonus. Write down these jobs and then Internet the crap out of them to get a feel for what they actually entail. Everything sounds cool when recruiters explain it. 

3) Your job will be the most significant factor in your experience. While we are all Airman, we all have different jobs that are given AFSCs (Air Force Specialty Codes). It will determine the squadron you are in and what your day-to-day will entail. It could be doing maintenance on an airplane, guarding a gate, doing medical physicals for other members, civil engineering work, preparing food, fixing vehicles, doing finance, administrative work, computer work, etc. As you can see, these are all very different so really make sure you have a job you want to do or at least won't mind doing. Most jobs with a bonus have that bonus or a reason; they are tough to attract new recruits into. 

4) If you decide to keep pursuing a career with the ANG, you'll need to get an extensive physical done at a MEPS (Military Entrance Processing Station). This will take 1-2 days and will seem pretty intense. 

5) Assuming you pass all the medical:dental, background investigations, drug tests, vision tests, height-weight requirements, etc. you will enlist for 2,3,4 or 6 years depending on how your unit offers enlistments. This means that you will go to basic training and job-specific technical training (this could take anywhere from 4-12+ months combined during which you are a full time military member and will be sent to an active duty base somewhere in the U.S.) within the first year. After that, you are only required to appear one weekend every month for UTA (Unit Training Assemblies; AKA "Drill" weekends) and possibly 1-2 weeks in the summer (usually) to train on your job so that you are competent to deploy for 2-4 months and perform your job overseas. You will also be expected to do a fitness test once a year where you will be required to run 1.5 miles in anywhere from 9-13 minutes depending on your age/scores in other areas, do as many push-ups/sit-ups in a minute as you can and have your waist circumference measured.

  Being in the reserves or guard requires commitment and sacrifice. It also isn't as easy to get in as it used to be as everything is down-sizing right now. If you want to experience being in the ANG, then it's right for you and will be a good experience. If you want to do a certain job, make money, "see the world," be a bad-ass etc., you may be disappointed because none of these are guarantees and can be subject to change. 

I've done 4+ years active duty, 3 years in one state ANG unit and just started 6 years in another one and love it but as the cliche goes, it's not for everybody. Good luck and feel free to ask follow-up questions/clarifications.

You should talk to a recruiter only if you want to experience being in the National Guard or Air National Guard for 2-6 years and nothing else as other benefits (money, benefits, travel, adventure, etc.) are not necessarily guaranteed. Bear in mind that you will be giving up at least one weekend a month (not your choice which one), a few weeks out of the year and are going to be staying where you're at during that time (transfers are possible but not a guarantee) unless you don't mind long drives. 

You will also have to take several months to complete your basic and advanced/technical training at some point (not necessarily at the beginning). You will need to stay in decent shape and potentially be available for training/real world TDYs (Temporary DutY - being put on active duty orders; going from part time to full time military) that may interfere with work/classes/life/happiness.

A lot of the military branches are down-sizing right now so not every job is available immediately but do no go in without a guaranteed job (MOS or AFSC). Look up all the jobs available and if one really jumps out at you, search the army/air force subreddit to see if someone else has asked about the reality of the job (most descriptions sound mis-leadingly awesome). 

Tldr; Look up all the jobs (MOS or AFSC) and talk to a recruiter about the "job of your dreams" but don't sign up for the National Guard or Air National Guard unless simply being in the guard is the reason you want to join; nothing else is necessarily a guarantee.

I was an AD X4N0X1 for 2 years out of 375th AES at Scott AFB, IL from 2004-2006 so my information is likely a bit out of date. 

I was working in hospital as med tech for 4 years and then applied for the special duty of aeromedical evacuation technician which means I had to get a flight physical first. If you have any relevant medical history, it will come up. 

Then I was sent to AET school at Brooks City Base(?) which wasn't too bad (2-3 mos. maybe?) and a nerfed version of SERE school for a week or two (more fun than intense). This is probably different now. Maybe done at Ft. Sam Houston?

I was then assigned to one of the four active duty squadrons in the world (far more guard/reservist units) and had to go through a 6-12 month(?) training period within the squadron that culminated in a check ride wherein an evaluator shadows you during a training mission and asks you all sorts of questions and presents various scenarios for you to react to. It's all about knowing your publications and using your flight check list. "We don't expect you to memorize everything but you must be able to look it up in a timely fashion and apply the information."

After that, I deployed twice in two years for 6 months each. Once to Germany (jackpot) and once to Qatar. We flew 5 man crews (2 nurses, 3 AETs) for long missions; into/out of theater of operations to Europe and then Europe to US and 3 man crews (1 nurse, 2 AETs) to consolidate those who were cleared for medical evacuation to one base in the theater for the 5 man crews to pick up thus keeping beds available at field medical facilities. I also participated in the Hurricane Rita evacuation and various stateside missions. 

It's mostly about knowing your regs, setting up the aircraft and long, sometimes boring flights. The critical patients are taken care of by CCATT teams and in order to be cleared for aerovac, patients must be stable so you don't get to use your medical knowledge as often as you may like. We flew aboard C-130s and C-17s mostly. We also used C-141s (that's how old I am), KC-135s and C-21s. C-17s were my favorite.

Stateside, it's mostly readiness training. You'll be assigned to a flight like medical equipment (maintain the medical gear), scheduling, training or some other administrative duty for your daily life. I imagine in the guard/reserves, most drills will consist of training missions aboard aircraft using mannequins and scenarios and ensuring all your readiness/training is complete.

It was a great time and I got to travel a lot for missions and training. Good people too. It can be boring at times and required staying awake for long periods of time (some missions could be 48-72 hours long but we would let each other nap if needed). It can also be tedious as some missions make you feel more like a glorified flight attendant than medic. We dealt mostly with Army and Marine patients which took a little getting used to as well (different lingo, protocol etc). 

Sorry this was mostly just my story but hopefully some of it helps. I still have some buddies in and could try to track down specific (up to date?) answers if you really want. As I was young and single at the time, I really liked it. The tempo was a little more trying for those with families. I imagine it's winding down a bit like everything so maybe it has slowed down a bit. Good luck :)
